findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add `.gitleaks.toml` to Scope, with a narrowly scoped allowlist (UUID env id right after `REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS` / `trusted_keys` only) so the compose and autodeploy trust-list values don't trip generic-api-key.
evidence: Plan Scope lists `infra/compose/docker-compose.yml`, `infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh` but not `.gitleaks.toml`

The working tree's .gitleaks.toml:88-99 carries an ADR 0125 allowlist: 'generic-api-key fires only because the identifier ends in "keys" and the first value token is the UUID env id', with regex `(?:REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS|trusted_keys)["':=,\s]{1,6}...[0-9a-f]{8}-...`

AC: 'the change lands through Gerrit with LLM-Review +1' — the review's gitleaks secret scan scans each changed file in full (see the existing .gitleaks.toml allowlist rationale: 'whole-file-scans a changed file ... would force-BLOCK')
findings.finding: Scope leaves out `.gitleaks.toml`, which the deployment step forces you to edit. Putting `<env_id> ssh-ed25519 <pubkey>` entries under `REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS` in docker-compose.yml, and in autodeploy's `trusted_keys` / `-e`, trips gitleaks' generic-api-key rule. It fires because the identifier ends in "keys" and the first value token is a UUID. A scoped allowlist entry is needed, or the secret scan force-blocks the change.
scenarios: An implementer following the plan's Scope edits only compose and autodeploy; the code-review secret scanner flags the UUID-prefixed values as a generic API key and blocks LLM-Review +1
A later edit to docker-compose.yml or autodeploy.sh re-triggers the whole-file scan and blocks again
findings.suggested_fix: In Approach step 5 and Scope, add: '`.gitleaks.toml`: a new `[[allowlists]]` entry (regexTarget = "match") matching only a UUID environment id directly after `REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS` or `trusted_keys`, with an ADR 0125 rationale; no path exclusion, so any other value under those identifiers still trips.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Move the SHA256 key-fingerprint computation into a shared lower-layer helper (e.g. in `_opcert_verify.py` or an sshsig util) used by both `fsck_authorship.signer_key_id` and the new `signing_key` field.
evidence: "the `SHA256:` fingerprint computed as `signer_key_id` in `src/rebar/_commands/fsck_authorship.py`"
findings.finding: The plan says `signing_key` is 'computed as `signer_key_id` in `src/rebar/_commands/fsck_authorship.py`' without saying whether to import it or reimplement it. Importing from `_commands` into the core `_opcert_verify` module inverts the layering. Reimplementing duplicates the fingerprint logic, and the two copies can drift.
scenarios: Someone later changes fingerprint normalisation in fsck_authorship; verify_signature `signing_key` silently diverges from fsck output.
findings.suggested_fix: Extract `signer_key_id`'s body into a function in a non-command module (e.g. `rebar.attest.sshsig`) and have both fsck_authorship and _opcert_verify call it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In Approach step 2, say that `signing_key` comes from a single shared 'public-key line → SHA256 fingerprint' helper used by both `fsck_authorship.signer_key_id` and `_opcert_verify`, instead of a re-implemented `_signing_key_sha256`.
evidence: Plan: "the `SHA256:` fingerprint computed as `signer_key_id` in `src/rebar/_commands/fsck_authorship.py`". It says 'computed as', not 'computed by' or 'shared helper'.

src/rebar/_commands/fsck_authorship.py:58-60: `blob = base64.b64decode(public_key.split(" ", 1)[1]); digest = base64.b64encode(hashlib.sha256(blob).digest()).decode("ascii"); return "SHA256:" + digest.rstrip("=")`

src/rebar/_opcert_verify.py:163-176: `_signing_key_sha256` repeats the same steps: `base64.b64decode(parts[1], validate=True)` … `"SHA256:" + base64.b64encode(hashlib.sha256(blob).digest()).decode("ascii").rstrip("=")`
A search for `"SHA256:" +` under src/rebar finds exactly these two implementations.
findings.finding: Approach step 2 defines `signing_key` as the `SHA256:` fingerprint 'computed as `signer_key_id` in `src/rebar/_commands/fsck_authorship.py`' but never says to reuse or factor out that existing computation. That leaves room for a second copy of the fingerprint logic, and one exists: `_opcert_verify._signing_key_sha256` repeats the base64-decode / sha256 / rstrip('=') formatting already in `fsck_authorship.signer_key_id`.
findings.location: Approach step 2 ('Every op-cert result gains `signing_key` … computed as `signer_key_id`'); src/rebar/_opcert_verify.py
scenarios: If someone later fixes the fingerprint format in one copy (for example padding handling or strict base64 validation, which already differ: one uses validate=True and the other does not), `verify_signature`'s `signing_key` will no longer match the key ids that `fsck`/`verify-identity` report for the same key.
An operator who cross-references an `untrusted` reason's fingerprint against `divergence_report` output sees different strings for the same key if the copies drift.
findings.suggested_fix: Move the line-to-fingerprint step (split the key line, base64-decode the body, sha256, unpadded base64, `SHA256:` prefix) into one helper, for example `public_key_fingerprint(line) -> str | None` next to `embedded_public_key` in `rebar.attest.sshsig`. Make `fsck_authorship.signer_key_id` call it after decoding the DSSE, and have `_opcert_verify` call it on `_embedded_signer_key(envelope)`. Then delete `_signing_key_sha256`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a rollback note: unsetting `REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS` in both deploy files (or reverting the change) restores pin-file trust via autodeploy, valid until the sibling story removes the pin file.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the default parse rule: split each entry on whitespace with maxsplit=3 (comment = remainder, spaces allowed, commas forbidden), and state whether env_id and key-type are validated.
evidence: "requires `<env_id> <key-type> <base64> [comment]` with decodable base64"
Step 5 comment "nava-opcert-prod rotated-20260907"
findings.finding: The entry grammar `<env_id> <key-type> <base64> [comment]` leaves several things unstated. Can the comment contain spaces? The deployed comment `nava-opcert-prod rotated-20260907` does. Can it contain commas? Commas would be split by the comma-separated env form. Is `env_id` validated, e.g. as a UUID? Is key-type restricted, e.g. to ssh-ed25519?
scenarios: The parser splits on all whitespace and rejects the 5-token rotated-key entry, or accepts a comma-containing comment and mis-splits the list.
findings.suggested_fix: Document: entries are split on ',' then each is `str.split(maxsplit=3)`; fewer than 3 fields, undecodable base64, or a key-type that mismatches the decoded blob raise ConfigError naming the 1-based entry position; comments may contain spaces but not commas.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Name the update owner for the trust list during the transition: document in docs/config.md (or the plan) that for the MCP deployment the compose/autodeploy value is authoritative and that rotations must update both infra files, not just the pin file.

'identical values listing the 3 keys now pinned'
'Out of scope: pin-file readers, the file, `rebar trusted-env` (sibling stories)'
findings.finding: Between this story's merge and the sibling story that stops reading the pin file, the MCP trust decision has two sources of truth: `.rebar/trusted_environments.yaml` (still maintained by `rebar trusted-env`) and the hard-coded list duplicated in docker-compose.yml and autodeploy.sh. Once the list is set, MCP ignores the pin file. A key added or rotated through `rebar trusted-env` therefore silently has no effect on the MCP server, and a rotation must edit two infra files. The plan names no update owner or rotation procedure for this window.

scenarios: An operator rotates a key with `rebar trusted-env` after this merge; the live MCP server returns `untrusted` for the new key because it reads only the deployment list.

findings.finding: The leaf hardcodes the three op-cert public keys as literal values in repo-tracked deployment files: the compose `mcp` environment and `-e` in autodeploy's `mcp_run_new`. Its deploy test then pins exactly those 3 (env_id, key body) pairs. This conflicts with the parent epic's operator decision that op-cert keys must not be hardcoded in the repository and that trust lives in the environment's own configuration, not in the repository. The epic's own decomposition comment approves the compose+autodeploy placement, so the parent contradicts itself. The leaf follows one parent clause and breaks the other.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In step 2, give the list-set verdict for (a) a decoded envelope with no principal and (b) an envelope with no extractable embedded key, and add both to the Testing list.
evidence: Plan: "Order: undecodable envelope `invalid`; bad signature `mismatch`; wrong signed subject `mismatch` ...; valid and bound but ... not listed: new verdict `untrusted`"
Plan: "Every op-cert result gains `signing_key` (null when no key can be extracted)". This admits a decodable envelope with no extractable key but gives no verdict for it.

src/rebar/_opcert_verify.py lines 312-318 (no principal → `foreign_key`) and 341-350 (list set, no signer key → `mismatch`) show the implementer had to make these calls without guidance from the plan.
findings.finding: The step 2 verdict order for the list-set case misses two branches that reach the trust check: an envelope that decodes but has no principal, and an envelope whose SSHSIG has no extractable embedded key. In both cases the stated trust root ('the SSHSIG's embedded key') cannot be used, and the plan doesn't say which verdict to return.
scenarios: A corrupted or non-SSHSIG signature reaches a list-set environment: one implementer returns `mismatch`, another `untrusted`, another `foreign_key`.
An MCP caller branching on the verdict gets different classifications for the same failure depending on who built it.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to step 2: "List set: a decoded envelope with no principal → `foreign_key` (unchanged); no extractable embedded key → `mismatch` (the signature cannot verify), with `signing_key` null."

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In steps 2-3, state the `trust_basis` value for list-set non-certified results (`untrusted`, `mismatch`) and update the trust_basis schema description to match.
evidence: Plan: "listed: passes, trust basis `trust_list`". No `trust_basis` is given for the `untrusted` or `mismatch` branches.
Plan step 3: "`trust_list` joins `trust_basis`". The schema description says trust_basis is 'Which key certified an op-cert record', so its meaning on a record that is not certified is unclear.

src/rebar/_opcert_verify.py line 351 sets `trust_basis = "envelope_key"` for every non-certified list-set result. That is a choice the plan never made, and `envelope_key` is the value audit readers are told means an unknown environment.
findings.finding: The plan defines `trust_basis: trust_list` only for the certified result. It doesn't say what `trust_basis` should be on list-set results that are not certified (`untrusted`, or `mismatch` from a bad signature or wrong subject). It also doesn't say whether the existing enum values (`own_key`, `pinned_environment`, `envelope_key`, null) may appear when the list is set.
scenarios: An audit reader sees an `untrusted` result with `trust_basis: envelope_key` and reads it as the embedded-key fallback from before the trust list.
Tests and the schema description disagree on whether trust_basis is null or set on failed list-set results.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In step 3, require that the plan_review_status.schema.json verdict description be updated to name `untrusted` among the signature-check verdicts, with the right count and a one-line meaning.
evidence: Plan: "`untrusted` joins the verdict enums of `src/rebar/schemas/verify_signature_result.schema.json` (described, in the unverified group) and `src/rebar/schemas/plan_review_status.schema.json`". 'Described' is attached only to the first schema.

src/rebar/schemas/plan_review_status.schema.json line 11 description: "The last 7 values (`mismatch`, `invalid`, `foreign_key`, `unavailable`, `unknown_kind`, `unknown_scheme`, `untrusted`) are the signature-check verdicts ...". This enumerated, counted list has to change whenever the enum changes.
findings.finding: Step 3 adds `untrusted` to the enum in plan_review_status.schema.json but says nothing about the verdict description. That description lists the signature-check verdicts by name and count ('The last N values (...)'), so it is the part LLM consumers read to classify verdicts. For verify_signature_result the plan explicitly says `untrusted` is '(described, in the unverified group)'; plan_review_status gets no such instruction.
scenarios: An executor appends `untrusted` to the enum only, leaving the description at 'The last 6 values' with `untrusted` unnamed, so the decision rule an LLM reads no longer matches the schema's own enum.
findings.suggested_fix: Change step 3 to: "... and `src/rebar/schemas/plan_review_status.schema.json` (added to the enumerated signature-check group in the verdict description, with its count updated and a one-line meaning)."

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that a malformed `verify.trusted_opcert_keys` leaves the MCP server up, makes `/health` `opcert` report `expected: true`, `matched: false` and an `error` naming the ConfigError, and add a health test for it.
evidence: "If the list cannot be read or coerced, the helper fails closed (`untrusted`, reason names the config error)"
Step 4 has no malformed-list case
Step 1: malformed entry "else `ConfigError`"
findings.finding: The plan defines fail-closed behaviour only for `verify_opcert_record`. It does not say what `opcert_signing_status`/`/health` reports when the list is malformed. It also does not say whether config load raises `ConfigError` at MCP server startup, which would take down the whole server rather than degrade op-cert only.
